title: The Comuna to the Butcher Shop: the Forger's Wife, the Miami Trade, and the Motorcycle
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Cartagena de Indias, the disputed birth
stops.date_confidence: 15 February 1943 is attested in both the English encyclopedia and the Biography profile. The place is not settled: Cartagena in the English account, Santa Marta in the Spanish, and no birth record has been produced by anyone consulted. The coordinate is the standard one for Cartagena de Indias and marks the city, not a house.
stops.campa: Cartagena de Indias on the Caribbean coast, February of 1943: a daughter is born to Ana Restrepo and is named Griselda. The city is a walled port that has moved contraband since the seventeenth century, and it is not where she grows up. The English encyclopedia gives Cartagena; her youngest son gives Santa Marta, two hundred kilometres east along the same coast. The record of the woman later called the godmother of the Miami cocaine trade opens with two cities and no document.
suggested_refs: Colombian civil registry records for Bolivar and Magdalena departments, 1943, not located in any source consulted

stops.name: Santa Marta, the other birthplace
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Spanish encyclopedia carries Michael Corleone Blanco's claim that Santa Marta and not Cartagena is his mother's birthplace, and does not adjudicate between the two. The date is carried over from the Cartagena entry; nothing separate attaches to it here.
stops.campa: Two hundred kilometres east of Cartagena, Santa Marta is the other candidate. Michael Corleone Blanco, the son who survives her, names this city as his mother's true birthplace, and the Spanish encyclopedia carries his account beside the Cartagena entry without preferring either. Neither city has produced a paper. She leaves the coast at about three and never lives on it again, so the question is settled by nobody and asked mainly by people writing about her death seventy years later.
suggested_refs: Michael Corleone Blanco's televised and printed accounts of his mother's origins

stops.name: Medellin, brought up into the valley
stops.date_confidence: the English encyclopedia gives her age as about three at the move with her mother Ana Restrepo, which places it around 1946. No month or day is recorded and the day defaults to the first. The coordinate is the city centre and no barrio is named in any source consulted.
stops.campa: Ana Restrepo carries her daughter up out of the coastal heat into the Aburra valley, to Medellin, a textile city climbing its own mountainsides in brick. Griselda is about three. The comunas she is raised in are the poorest ground in the most industrious city in the country, and every biographer reaches for the same explanation at the same point in the story. Sixty-six years later she is shot dead a few kilometres from where she is set down as a child.
suggested_refs: The postwar migration into Medellin's hillside comunas, 1940s

stops.name: Medellin city centre, the pickpocket
stops.date_confidence: the English encyclopedia places the pickpocketing before her teens rather than in them, so the window opens around 1953 and the research pool's framing of it as teenage work is corrected here. Year approximate, day defaulted to the first.
stops.campa: Downtown Medellin, the market blocks and the streets around the old parish square: she works them as a pickpocket before she is out of childhood. The English encyclopedia puts the trade before her teens rather than in them. Nothing about it is unusual for a girl of the comunas in the early 1950s, and nothing about it forecasts what follows. The work is done in crowds and rewards a child who can read one. It is also the first thing anybody records her doing for money.

stops.name: Medellin, the story of the kidnapped boy
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, single source. The story reaches the encyclopedia through Charles Cosby, a partner of her prison years, and the encyclopedia itself flags it as alleged. No police record, no name for the boy, no date beyond her approximate age of eleven. Nothing here is attested and the pin is the same central-city approximation as the previous stop.
stops.campa: One story attaches itself to her childhood and will not come off. Charles Cosby, a partner of her prison years, tells it: that at about eleven she helped take a boy from a wealthy family and shot him herself when the ransom was not paid. It rests on one man's telling, decades after, about a woman he met in custody. The encyclopedia carries it flagged as alleged. Every screen treatment of her life opens with it. It explains everything about her and can be checked by nobody.

stops.name: Medellin, married to the forger
stops.date_confidence: the English encyclopedia states she married Carlos Trujillo at about thirteen, which places the marriage around 1956. The research pool carried this as a first meeting in 1956 with a marriage in the 1960s; both halves of that are corrected here. No certificate has been published and the day defaults to the first.
stops.campa: At about thirteen she marries Carlos Trujillo, a forger of documents in Medellin. She is a child and he is a grown man with a trade. It is the first of the trades that will carry her out of Colombia: papers saying a person is someone else, made for anyone with the money to leave. The forger is, in the accounts, the man who teaches her that a border is a sheet of paper and a press. She crosses the United States border on his product in 1964 and never once crosses it under her own name.

stops.name: Medellin, the three sons of Carlos Trujillo
stops.date_confidence: Dixon, Uber and Osvaldo are named by the English encyclopedia, the Spanish encyclopedia and the Biography profile alike. stops.name: Medellin, out of her mother's house

Between the girl thieving in the centre of Medellin and the woman indicted in New York with thirty subordinates, the record keeps a forger's trade and a marriage nobody has produced the certificate for. stops.name: Bogota, the false papers trade
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Bogota forgery operation is a recurring detail in journalistic profiles, including retrospectives written around the Netflix series, and no primary document has been located for it. The early to middle 1960s is the window those profiles give; the year and day here are placeholders.
stops.campa: Bogota, the capital on the altiplano, is where the profiles put the forgery operation: passports made for people who want to be in the United States. The detail is repeated everywhere and rests on no document anyone has produced. The route it opens is the route she keeps for forty years, first people and then powder, moved on paperwork rather than in the dark. The ministries that issue the stamps are in Bogota, which is why the trade in forging them is. The pin is the city and not a workshop, because no workshop is named.
suggested_refs: Journalistic retrospectives on the Blanco and Trujillo document operation, none citing a primary record
sources: Press retrospectives on Griselda Blanco published around the 2024 Netflix series

stops.name: Queens, entry on documents that are not hers
stops.date_confidence: 1964 is attested by the English encyclopedia for the illegal entry and the settlement in Queens with her three sons and her second husband Alberto Bravo. stops.name: Jackson Heights, the couriers
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Journalistic accounts centre her New York operation on Jackson Heights in the late 1960s and early 1970s and describe cocaine carried in clothing and furniture, but no address and no dated record appears in the sources consulted. The neighbourhood is a working immigrant grid of six storey brick under elevated track, and the trade runs through its apartments the way older trades ran through the Lower East Side, on relatives and on credit nobody writes down.

stops.name: New York, the thing itself is built
stops.date_confidence: the 1970s New York cocaine operation with Alberto Bravo is attested in outline by both the encyclopedia and the Biography profile. No year is fixed for any stage of it, so 1972 stands as a midpoint between the 1964 arrival and the April 1975 indictment.
stops.campa: With Alberto Bravo, himself a trafficker, she builds the thing itself: suppliers in Colombia, couriers on the New York flights, distribution through the boroughs. Cocaine in the early 1970s is a small luxury market that no federal agency is organised to fight, and the organisation assembled inside it is run by a woman, which is the detail every later account leads with. In three years it is large enough that a grand jury needs thirty other names to describe it.

stops.name: Lower Manhattan, Operation Banshee
stops.date_confidence: April 1975 is attested for the federal indictment of Blanco and roughly thirty subordinates in the investigation called Operation Banshee; no day is given. The research pool assigned the case to the Southern District of New York, which no source states and which sits oddly with a Queens operation lying in the Eastern District. stops.campa: Federal prosecutors indict her and some thirty of her subordinates on drug conspiracy charges in the investigation called Operation Banshee. It is the first time the United States government writes her name on a charging document, and she does not appear to answer it; the family is on a plane to Colombia. Manuel Noriega is at this date the chief of Panamanian military intelligence, thirteen years from the Miami indictment that will name the same cargo moving the same way north.

stops.name: Outside Bogota, the killing of Alberto Bravo
stops.date_confidence: 1975 only, day defaulted to the first, though the event follows the April indictment and the flight from New York and should be read as later in the year. Biography places it outside Bogota without naming the site, so the city coordinate stands in. The killing of several of Bravo's associates in the same encounter is given by some accounts only.

She is thirty-two, a fugitive from a United States indictment, and now sole owner of the routes the two of them built. Nothing about the killing reaches a Colombian court. The operation continues without a pause, which is the only evidence anybody offers of who had been running it.

stops.name: Medellin, the son named Corleone
stops.date_confidence: 5 August 1978 in Medellin is the attested birth of Michael Corleone Blanco, son of her third husband Dario Sepulveda. The research pool placed the marriage in the early 1980s and the birth in Miami; both are wrong and are corrected here, which puts the marriage in the middle to late 1970s.
stops.campa: Medellin, the fifth of August 1978: Michael Corleone Blanco is born, son of her third husband Dario Sepulveda, named for the heir in the film that had opened six years earlier. He is the only one of her four sons who outlives her, and he is four years old when his father is shot dead in this same city. The name is chosen in the years when her trade is turning the word godmother into a job description, and he grows up to carry it on Miami television as the last living witness with an interest in the version he tells.

stops.name: Miami, the return and the new operation
stops.date_confidence: the encyclopedia and the Biography profile agree on a return to the United States in the latter half of the 1970s and the establishment of a major Miami operation, without fixing a year. stops.campa: She comes back into the United States and rebuilds in Miami as the city becomes the port of entry for Colombian cocaine. Meyer Lansky is alive on Collins Avenue, walking his dog, the Havana casinos of Charles Lucky Luciano's era thirty years behind him. The corridor their generation ran from Cuba into Florida is the corridor hers now floods with a product neither of them touched. stops.name: Miami, the killing of Johnny Castro
